follow_up_questions.question: Are the palms, the backs of your hands, or the skin between your fingers most affected?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 9] Patient: All over my arms, um, and my hands mainly.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Precise hand distribution helps distinguish types of dermatitis and other causes: irritant contact dermatitis and hand eczema often affect palms and fingertips; allergic contact dermatitis can involve backs of hands or contact sites; tinea/manuum often involves web spaces. This clarifies differential diagnosis and informs management.

follow_up_questions.question: How soon after swimming did the rash begin — within minutes, within a few hours, or the next day?
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Latency between exposure and onset differentiates immediate reactions (minutes–hours) such as acute allergic contact urticaria/allergic reaction versus delayed contact dermatitis or irritant reactions that typically occur hours to days later. This is key to linking the swimming exposure to an allergic or irritant cause of dermatitis.

follow_up_questions.question: Are there any small blisters or fluid-filled bumps on the rash?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 17] Patient: Um, so my skin's quite red, um, and I'm using coconut butter for the past few days.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Presence of vesicles or weeping suggests acute eczematous/vesicular dermatitis (often allergic contact or acute atopic flare) versus simple xerosis or chronic lichenified eczema. This finding would influence diagnosis and use of topical steroid potency and wet dressings.

follow_up_questions.question: Did you use any new sunscreen, body lotion, or hair product before or while you were swimming?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 29] Patient: , I went swimming a few days ago.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Topical products are common causes of allergic contact dermatitis and can be more likely than pool chemicals in some cases. Identifying a new product supports allergic contact dermatitis and guides avoidance and patch testing if needed.

follow_up_questions.question: At work, do you frequently use hand sanitiser, wash your hands many times per day, or handle cleaning products?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 23] Patient: Um, I work as a teacher.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Frequent handwashing, sanitiser use or exposure to cleaning agents (wet work/irritants) predispose to irritant contact dermatitis of the hands. This distinguishes occupational irritant dermatitis from atopic or allergic causes and suggests preventive measures (gloves, emollients).

follow_up_questions.question: Did you have eczema, asthma, or hayfever (allergic rhinitis) when you were a child?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 71] Patient: Um, yeah, so um, my dad has asthma, and, my mum has hayfever.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: A personal history of atopic disease (childhood eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis) increases the likelihood of atopic dermatitis. Family atopy is supportive but personal history is more specific for atopic predisposition.

follow_up_questions.question: Do you feel any burning or stinging on the affected skin, or is it purely itchy?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 19] Patient: I don't have any spots, and no fever , and I'm not sweating either.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Burning or stinging suggests chemical/irritant dermatitis or acute inflammation, whereas predominant itch with scratching is more typical of eczematous (atopic/allergic) dermatitis or scabies. This helps narrow cause and choice of symptomatic treatment.

follow_up_questions.question: Is the itching worse at night or does it wake you from sleep?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 7] Patient: Um, so basically, I've been really stressed at work for the past few days. And, I've realised that I've got, really dry itchy skin.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Nocturnal worsening of itch is characteristic of eczema and scabies; absence of nocturnal itch makes scabies less likely. This helps prioritize eczematous diagnoses and prompt contact tracing if scabies suspected.

follow_up_questions.question: Are any other areas affected now — your face, chest, legs, or is it only your hands and arms?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 14] Doctor: OK. And, has this spread anywhere else? Has it spread to your, to your chest, your legs, your face?
follow_up_questions.reasoning: Extent of spread differentiates localized contact dermatitis (usually limited to contact sites) from more generalized dermatitis or atopic flare. Widespread involvement would prompt consideration of systemic causes or more severe atopic dermatitis.

follow_up_questions.question: Have you ever had a similar skin reaction after swimming in the past?
follow_up_questions.quoted_excerpt: [ Turn ID 31] Patient: Uh, no, I've been before.
follow_up_questions.reasoning: A recurrent reaction specifically after swimming suggests a reproducible allergic or irritant reaction to pool chemicals or a product used for swimming. A one-off event makes an isolated irritant exposure more likely. This informs counseling and avoidance strategies.
